lessons.title: Control plane and reconciliation
lessons.summary: Kubernetes is a declarative orchestration system whose controllers reconcile observed state toward desired state stored through the API.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Kubernetes is a declarative orchestration system whose controllers reconcile observed state toward desired state stored through the API.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: The API server validates requests, etcd persists cluster state, controllers manage resource lifecycles, and the scheduler assigns unscheduled Pods. Reconciliation is asynchronous; creating an object does not guarantee its workload is already ready.

lessons.takeaway: The API server validates requests, etcd persists cluster state, controllers manage resource lifecycles, and the scheduler assigns unscheduled Pods. Reconciliation is asynchronous; creating an object does not guarantee its workload is already ready.

references.title: Control plane and reconciliation — primary documentation

lessons.title: Pods and containers
lessons.summary: A Pod is Kubernetes' scheduling unit containing one or more cooperating containers.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: A Pod is Kubernetes' scheduling unit containing one or more cooperating containers.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Containers in a Pod share its network namespace and can share declared volumes. Pods are disposable and normally replaced by controllers rather than repaired in place. A Pod IP is not a stable service address.

lessons.takeaway: Containers in a Pod share its network namespace and can share declared volumes. Pods are disposable and normally replaced by controllers rather than repaired in place. A Pod IP is not a stable service address.

lessons.title: Deployments and ReplicaSets
lessons.summary: A Deployment manages ReplicaSets to maintain and update replicated stateless Pods.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: A Deployment manages ReplicaSets to maintain and update replicated stateless Pods.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Changing the Pod template creates a new rollout. Rolling-update settings control surge and unavailable capacity. A ReplicaSet count does not prove application readiness; inspect conditions, readiness and available replicas.

lessons.takeaway: Changing the Pod template creates a new rollout. Rolling-update settings control surge and unavailable capacity. A ReplicaSet count does not prove application readiness; inspect conditions, readiness and available replicas.

lessons.title: StatefulSets
lessons.summary: A StatefulSet manages Pods with stable identities and ordered lifecycle behavior appropriate to some stateful applications.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: A StatefulSet manages Pods with stable identities and ordered lifecycle behavior appropriate to some stateful applications.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Each ordinal can retain a distinct volume claim and network identity. The application still owns replication and data consistency. Replacing a Pod does not automatically repair corrupted data or guarantee a safe database failover.

lessons.takeaway: Each ordinal can retain a distinct volume claim and network identity. The application still owns replication and data consistency. Replacing a Pod does not automatically repair corrupted data or guarantee a safe database failover.

lessons.title: DaemonSets
lessons.summary: A DaemonSet maintains a Pod on eligible nodes, commonly for networking, logs or host agents.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: A DaemonSet maintains a Pod on eligible nodes, commonly for networking, logs or host agents.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Node selectors, affinity and tolerations influence eligibility. A daemon rollout can affect every node, so monitor availability and resource use. DaemonSets are not a substitute for ordinary replicated application Deployments.

lessons.takeaway: Node selectors, affinity and tolerations influence eligibility. A daemon rollout can affect every node, so monitor availability and resource use. DaemonSets are not a substitute for ordinary replicated application Deployments.

lessons.title: Jobs and CronJobs
lessons.summary: A Job manages work intended to complete; a CronJob creates Jobs according to a schedule.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: A Job manages work intended to complete; a CronJob creates Jobs according to a schedule.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Retries, deadlines and concurrency policy affect execution. Work should tolerate duplicate or retried execution where applicable. Successful Pod completion is not proof that an external business operation occurred exactly once.

lessons.takeaway: Retries, deadlines and concurrency policy affect execution. Work should tolerate duplicate or retried execution where applicable. Successful Pod completion is not proof that an external business operation occurred exactly once.

lessons.title: Namespaces
lessons.summary: Namespaces scope names and selected policies for groups of Kubernetes objects.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Namespaces scope names and selected policies for groups of Kubernetes objects.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: They help organize workloads and apply quotas or permissions, but are not complete security boundaries by themselves. Some resources are cluster-scoped. Network and identity isolation require additional controls.

lessons.takeaway: They help organize workloads and apply quotas or permissions, but are not complete security boundaries by themselves. Some resources are cluster-scoped. Network and identity isolation require additional controls.

lessons.title: Labels and selectors
lessons.summary: Labels attach identifying attributes to objects; selectors choose objects by those attributes.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Labels attach identifying attributes to objects; selectors choose objects by those attributes.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Services and controllers rely on matching selectors, so accidental label changes can disconnect traffic or change ownership behavior. Use stable labels for identity and separate changing metadata. A matching label does not imply a Pod is ready.

lessons.takeaway: Services and controllers rely on matching selectors, so accidental label changes can disconnect traffic or change ownership behavior. Use stable labels for identity and separate changing metadata. A matching label does not imply a Pod is ready.

lessons.title: Services and EndpointSlices
lessons.summary: A Service provides a stable access abstraction for selected backends; EndpointSlices describe backend addresses and readiness information.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: A Service provides a stable access abstraction for selected backends; EndpointSlices describe backend addresses and readiness information.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Selectors commonly populate EndpointSlices from Pods. Service port and targetPort serve different roles. When traffic fails, verify selectors, ready endpoints and the application's actual listening port before changing exposure type.

lessons.takeaway: Selectors commonly populate EndpointSlices from Pods. Service port and targetPort serve different roles. When traffic fails, verify selectors, ready endpoints and the application's actual listening port before changing exposure type.

lessons.title: Cluster DNS
lessons.summary: Cluster DNS provides service discovery names within the Kubernetes networking environment.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Cluster DNS provides service discovery names within the Kubernetes networking environment.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Pod resolver configuration and search domains influence name lookup. Service discovery requires DNS health as well as correctly named resources. A successful lookup establishes an address, not application reachability or readiness.

lessons.takeaway: Pod resolver configuration and search domains influence name lookup. Service discovery requires DNS health as well as correctly named resources. A successful lookup establishes an address, not application reachability or readiness.

lessons.title: Ingress and Gateway
lessons.summary: Ingress and Gateway API resources describe routing from clients toward services through implementing controllers.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Ingress and Gateway API resources describe routing from clients toward services through implementing controllers.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Creating a routing object alone does not install a controller or load balancer. Listener, hostname, route attachment, TLS and backend health all affect delivery. Supported features depend on the chosen implementation.

lessons.takeaway: Creating a routing object alone does not install a controller or load balancer. Listener, hostname, route attachment, TLS and backend health all affect delivery. Supported features depend on the chosen implementation.

lessons.title: NetworkPolicy
lessons.summary: NetworkPolicy declares allowed traffic relationships for Pods when enforced by a supporting network plugin.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: NetworkPolicy declares allowed traffic relationships for Pods when enforced by a supporting network plugin.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Ingress and egress isolation are evaluated separately, and allowed policies combine. Include required DNS and dependency paths when restricting egress. A policy object without an enforcing implementation does not block packets.

lessons.takeaway: Ingress and egress isolation are evaluated separately, and allowed policies combine. Include required DNS and dependency paths when restricting egress. A policy object without an enforcing implementation does not block packets.

lessons.title: ConfigMaps
lessons.summary: A ConfigMap stores non-secret configuration data separately from container images.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: A ConfigMap stores non-secret configuration data separately from container images.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Values can be injected as environment variables or mounted files. Environment variables do not update in an already running container when the ConfigMap changes. Application reload behavior and mount update semantics determine when changes take effect.

lessons.takeaway: Values can be injected as environment variables or mounted files. Environment variables do not update in an already running container when the ConfigMap changes. Application reload behavior and mount update semantics determine when changes take effect.

lessons.title: Secrets
lessons.summary: A Secret stores sensitive configuration values for authorized workload access.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: A Secret stores sensitive configuration values for authorized workload access.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Base64 representation is encoding, not encryption. Control RBAC, encryption-at-rest configuration, mount exposure and log handling. Updating a Secret does not guarantee every application immediately reloads its credentials.

lessons.takeaway: Base64 representation is encoding, not encryption. Control RBAC, encryption-at-rest configuration, mount exposure and log handling. Updating a Secret does not guarantee every application immediately reloads its credentials.

lessons.title: Service accounts
lessons.summary: A ServiceAccount identifies a workload for Kubernetes API authentication and related identity integration.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: A ServiceAccount identifies a workload for Kubernetes API authentication and related identity integration.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: RBAC determines what the identity can do. Avoid mounting credentials where API access is unnecessary, and use appropriately scoped, bounded tokens. A namespace's default service account should not silently become a broad administrative identity.

lessons.takeaway: RBAC determines what the identity can do. Avoid mounting credentials where API access is unnecessary, and use appropriately scoped, bounded tokens. A namespace's default service account should not silently become a broad administrative identity.

lessons.title: RBAC
lessons.summary: Role-based access control authorizes API operations through roles and bindings.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Role-based access control authorizes API operations through roles and bindings.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Roles define verbs on resources, while bindings grant those permissions to subjects. Namespace and cluster scope matter. Check the exact verb, resource and identity rather than treating authentication success as authorization.

lessons.command: kubectl auth can-i get pods -n NAMESPACE
lessons.takeaway: Roles define verbs on resources, while bindings grant those permissions to subjects. Namespace and cluster scope matter. Check the exact verb, resource and identity rather than treating authentication success as authorization.

lessons.title: Requests and limits
lessons.summary: Resource requests inform scheduling and resource sharing; limits constrain resource use according to the resource type.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Resource requests inform scheduling and resource sharing; limits constrain resource use according to the resource type.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: CPU limits may throttle runnable work, while memory pressure against a limit can lead to OOM termination. Current usage is not the scheduler's capacity calculation. Compare workload demand, requests, limits and node conditions.

lessons.takeaway: CPU limits may throttle runnable work, while memory pressure against a limit can lead to OOM termination. Current usage is not the scheduler's capacity calculation. Compare workload demand, requests, limits and node conditions.

lessons.title: Scheduling and affinity
lessons.summary: The scheduler selects a feasible node for an unscheduled Pod using resource and placement constraints.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: The scheduler selects a feasible node for an unscheduled Pod using resource and placement constraints.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Requests, affinity, topology rules, volumes and other filters affect feasibility. Hard constraints can leave Pods Pending even when aggregate capacity looks sufficient. Inspect scheduling events before relaxing intended placement rules.

lessons.takeaway: Requests, affinity, topology rules, volumes and other filters affect feasibility. Hard constraints can leave Pods Pending even when aggregate capacity looks sufficient. Inspect scheduling events before relaxing intended placement rules.

lessons.title: Taints and tolerations
lessons.summary: Taints repel Pods from nodes unless matching tolerations permit the placement.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Taints repel Pods from nodes unless matching tolerations permit the placement.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: A toleration permits scheduling but does not attract a Pod to that node. Combine with affinity when dedicated placement is required. Effects such as NoSchedule and NoExecute influence new placement and eviction differently.

lessons.takeaway: A toleration permits scheduling but does not attract a Pod to that node. Combine with affinity when dedicated placement is required. Effects such as NoSchedule and NoExecute influence new placement and eviction differently.

lessons.title: Readiness liveness and startup probes
lessons.summary: Probes communicate whether a container is ready for traffic, needs restart, or is still starting.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Probes communicate whether a container is ready for traffic, needs restart, or is still starting.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Readiness failures remove a Pod from ordinary ready service backends; liveness failure can restart the container. Startup probes delay other probes until startup succeeds. A dependency outage should not automatically cause a fleet-wide restart loop.

lessons.takeaway: Readiness failures remove a Pod from ordinary ready service backends; liveness failure can restart the container. Startup probes delay other probes until startup succeeds. A dependency outage should not automatically cause a fleet-wide restart loop.

references.title: Readiness liveness and startup probes — primary documentation

lessons.title: Persistent volumes and claims
lessons.summary: A PersistentVolume represents storage capacity; a PersistentVolumeClaim requests storage for a workload.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: A PersistentVolume represents storage capacity; a PersistentVolumeClaim requests storage for a workload.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Binding, access modes, topology and reclaim policy affect allocation and lifecycle. A claim can remain Pending because no suitable storage is provisioned. Deleting workload objects and deleting data are separate operations with policy-dependent consequences.

lessons.takeaway: Binding, access modes, topology and reclaim policy affect allocation and lifecycle. A claim can remain Pending because no suitable storage is provisioned. Deleting workload objects and deleting data are separate operations with policy-dependent consequences.

references.title: Persistent volumes and claims — primary documentation

lessons.title: StorageClasses and CSI
lessons.summary: A StorageClass describes provisioning parameters, while CSI drivers implement storage operations.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: A StorageClass describes provisioning parameters, while CSI drivers implement storage operations.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Binding mode can coordinate volume placement with Pod scheduling. Driver health, permissions and zone constraints influence provisioning and attachment. A provisioned volume still needs a valid filesystem and application-consistent data procedures.

lessons.takeaway: Binding mode can coordinate volume placement with Pod scheduling. Driver health, permissions and zone constraints influence provisioning and attachment. A provisioned volume still needs a valid filesystem and application-consistent data procedures.

lessons.title: Horizontal Pod Autoscaling
lessons.summary: An HPA adjusts replica counts from configured metrics and scaling rules.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: An HPA adjusts replica counts from configured metrics and scaling rules.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Metrics availability, resource requests, stabilization and replica bounds affect decisions. More replicas only help if the bottleneck can scale horizontally. Inspect HPA conditions and downstream capacity before raising maximum replicas.

lessons.takeaway: Metrics availability, resource requests, stabilization and replica bounds affect decisions. More replicas only help if the bottleneck can scale horizontally. Inspect HPA conditions and downstream capacity before raising maximum replicas.

lessons.title: Disruption budgets
lessons.summary: A PodDisruptionBudget limits selected voluntary disruptions according to desired availability.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: A PodDisruptionBudget limits selected voluntary disruptions according to desired availability.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: It can constrain eviction during maintenance but does not prevent all failures or guarantee application quorum. Too-strict budgets can block drains. Align the selector and availability setting with replica count and application behavior.

lessons.takeaway: It can constrain eviction during maintenance but does not prevent all failures or guarantee application quorum. Too-strict budgets can block drains. Align the selector and availability setting with replica count and application behavior.

lessons.title: Node lifecycle and drain
lessons.summary: Node lifecycle operations control scheduling and safely remove workloads during maintenance.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Node lifecycle operations control scheduling and safely remove workloads during maintenance.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Cordon prevents new ordinary scheduling; drain uses eviction subject to relevant constraints. DaemonSets, local data and disruption budgets require explicit handling. Confirm replacement capacity before removing a node from service.

lessons.takeaway: Cordon prevents new ordinary scheduling; drain uses eviction subject to relevant constraints. DaemonSets, local data and disruption budgets require explicit handling. Confirm replacement capacity before removing a node from service.

references.title: Node lifecycle and drain — primary documentation

lessons.title: Security contexts
lessons.summary: Security contexts configure process identity and privilege-related runtime settings for Pods or containers.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Security contexts configure process identity and privilege-related runtime settings for Pods or containers.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Non-root execution, capability reduction, read-only roots and seccomp profiles restrict different behaviors. Volume ownership and application write paths must remain compatible. Avoid privileged mode as a general fix for permission errors.

lessons.command: kubectl get pod POD -n NAMESPACE -o yaml
lessons.takeaway: Non-root execution, capability reduction, read-only roots and seccomp profiles restrict different behaviors. Volume ownership and application write paths must remain compatible. Avoid privileged mode as a general fix for permission errors.

lessons.title: Admission and policy
lessons.summary: Admission evaluates API requests after authentication and authorization and before persistence.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Admission evaluates API requests after authentication and authorization and before persistence.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Built-in controllers and webhooks can validate or mutate objects. A failing webhook can block otherwise authorized changes depending on policy. Diagnose rejection messages and webhook availability rather than broadly disabling safeguards.

lessons.takeaway: Built-in controllers and webhooks can validate or mutate objects. A failing webhook can block otherwise authorized changes depending on policy. Diagnose rejection messages and webhook availability rather than broadly disabling safeguards.

lessons.title: Rollouts and rollback
lessons.summary: A rollout replaces workload revisions; rollback returns the Pod template to an earlier revision when available.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: A rollout replaces workload revisions; rollback returns the Pod template to an earlier revision when available.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Deployment success reflects controller progress, not every business transaction. Data migrations and external configuration may not roll back with the template. Compare application health and dependency compatibility before and after recovery.

lessons.takeaway: Deployment success reflects controller progress, not every business transaction. Data migrations and external configuration may not roll back with the template. Compare application health and dependency compatibility before and after recovery.

lessons.title: Observability and events
lessons.summary: Kubernetes events, logs and metrics expose different parts of workload behavior.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Kubernetes events, logs and metrics expose different parts of workload behavior.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Events describe controller and node observations but expire; container logs show application output; metrics reveal trends. Correlate them by object, timestamp and revision. Absence of retained events does not prove an incident never occurred.

lessons.takeaway: Events describe controller and node observations but expire; container logs show application output; metrics reveal trends. Correlate them by object, timestamp and revision. Absence of retained events does not prove an incident never occurred.

lessons.title: etcd and disaster recovery
lessons.summary: etcd stores Kubernetes cluster state, while application data usually lives in separate storage systems.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: etcd stores Kubernetes cluster state, while application data usually lives in separate storage systems.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Protect and test control-plane backups using the distribution's supported procedures. Restoring etcd does not restore every database volume or external cloud dependency. Recovery plans must cover certificates, identities, networking and application data as well as API objects.

lessons.takeaway: Protect and test control-plane backups using the distribution's supported procedures. Restoring etcd does not restore every database volume or external cloud dependency. Recovery plans must cover certificates, identities, networking and application data as well as API objects.

references.title: etcd and disaster recovery — primary documentation

commands.title: Current cluster context
commands.purpose: Confirm the cluster identity before interacting with workloads.
commands.environment: Read-only local command; a friendly name is not proof of the underlying endpoint.
commands.interpretation: The context name is local configuration; inspect its cluster and namespace if ambiguous.
commands.safety: Read-only local command; a friendly name is not proof of the underlying endpoint.

commands.title: List Pods
commands.definition: Lists Pods with readiness, restarts, IP and node placement.
commands.purpose: Compare affected replicas and shared nodes.
commands.environment: Read-only; replace NAMESPACE with the intended scope.
commands.expectedOutput: NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE IP NODE
commands.interpretation: READY is ready containers over total; STATUS is summarized state, and NODE shows placement.
commands.safety: Read-only; replace NAMESPACE with the intended scope.

commands.title: Describe Pod
commands.definition: Shows Pod configuration, conditions, container state and events.
commands.purpose: Distinguish scheduling, image, probe and storage failures.
commands.environment: Read-only; output may include sensitive configuration metadata.
commands.interpretation: Read Conditions, Last State and Events together; Warning reasons often point to the next check.
commands.safety: Read-only; output may include sensitive configuration metadata.

commands.title: Current logs
commands.definition: Reads a bounded log tail with timestamps.
commands.purpose: Correlate application errors with the incident.
commands.environment: Read-only; redact credentials and personal data before sharing.
commands.interpretation: Each line is application output; use -c CONTAINER when selection is ambiguous.
commands.safety: Read-only; redact credentials and personal data before sharing.

commands.title: Previous container logs
commands.definition: Reads the previous terminated container instance's available logs.
commands.purpose: Find the error that caused a restart rather than only current startup messages.
commands.expectedOutput: fatal: configuration could not be loaded
commands.interpretation: A previous instance must exist and logs must still be retained.

commands.title: Recent events
commands.definition: Lists retained namespace events ordered by last timestamp.
commands.environment: Read-only; event retention is limited, so absence is not proof of no failure.
commands.interpretation: Reason and Message identify observations; repeated events may be aggregated and timestamps have limitations.
commands.safety: Read-only; event retention is limited, so absence is not proof of no failure.

commands.title: Service definition
commands.definition: Shows selectors, ports and service metadata.
commands.purpose: Check whether routing selects the intended Pods and target port.
commands.environment: Read-only; service existence does not prove backend readiness.
commands.interpretation: Selector must match labels; Port and TargetPort have different roles.
commands.safety: Read-only; service existence does not prove backend readiness.

commands.title: Service endpoints
commands.command: kubectl get endpointslices -n NAMESPACE -l kubernetes.io/service-name=SERVICE -o yaml
commands.definition: Shows EndpointSlices associated with one Service.
commands.purpose: Verify backend addresses and readiness conditions.
commands.environment: Read-only; EndpointSlices may include not-ready or terminating endpoints.
commands.interpretation: Inspect addresses, ports and conditions.ready for each endpoint.
commands.safety: Read-only; EndpointSlices may include not-ready or terminating endpoints.

commands.title: Rollout status
commands.definition: Observes deployment progress with a bounded wait.
commands.purpose: Detect a stalled rollout without waiting indefinitely.
commands.environment: Read-only observation; still verify user-facing behavior.
commands.interpretation: Success means controller rollout completion; a timeout requires Pod and Deployment inspection.
commands.safety: Read-only observation; still verify user-facing behavior.

commands.title: Resource usage
commands.definition: Shows recent Pod CPU and memory measurements.
commands.purpose: Compare consumption across replicas and with configured limits.
commands.environment: Read-only; requires a functioning metrics API.
commands.interpretation: CPU is commonly shown in millicores and memory in binary units; this is not a historical peak.
commands.safety: Read-only; requires a functioning metrics API.

commands.title: Permission check
commands.command: kubectl auth can-i get pods -n NAMESPACE
commands.definition: Asks whether the current identity may perform the specified operation.
commands.purpose: Distinguish authorization failures from network or authentication errors.
commands.environment: Read-only authorization review; impersonation options require separate privileges.
commands.interpretation: yes applies to that verb, resource and scope, not unrestricted cluster access.
commands.safety: Read-only authorization review; impersonation options require separate privileges.

commands.title: Storage claims
commands.definition: Lists persistent-volume claims and binding status.
commands.purpose: Identify unbound storage blocking a workload.
commands.environment: Read-only; inspect claim events and storage topology next if Pending.
commands.expectedOutput: NAME STATUS VOLUME CAPACITY ACCESS MODES STORAGECLASS
commands.interpretation: STATUS Bound means a volume association exists; it does not prove attachment, mount or data health.
commands.safety: Read-only; inspect claim events and storage topology next if Pending.

debugging.title: Pod remains Pending
debugging.symptom: A new Pod never receives a node assignment.

steps.evidence: Read scheduling conditions and events for requests, taints, affinity, topology or unbound claims. Aggregate idle CPU does not prove a feasible node exists.
Correct the evidenced request or placement mistake, provision appropriate capacity or resolve storage binding. Preserve intentional isolation constraints.
Confirm scheduling, readiness and application health, and verify the Pod landed in the intended failure domain.

debugging.title: CrashLoopBackOff
debugging.symptom: A container repeatedly starts and exits.

steps.evidence: Combine previous logs with last termination state and events. Distinguish application exit, OOM, failed liveness and missing configuration.
Fix or roll back the evidenced application/configuration regression; tune resources or probes only when supported by measurements.
Verify restart count stabilizes and representative traffic succeeds across the rollout, including startup and shutdown.

debugging.title: ImagePullBackOff
debugging.symptom: A Pod cannot retrieve its configured image.

steps.evidence: Read pull error details and confirm image reference, digest/tag, registry authorization and node network path. Different errors require different fixes.
Correct the reference or image-pull identity, restore registry reachability or publish the intended image. Avoid embedding registry credentials in manifests.
Confirm the intended image digest runs and all eligible nodes can pull through the approved path.

debugging.title: Service has no ready backends
debugging.symptom: A Service exists but requests have no available backend.

steps.command: kubectl get endpointslices -n NAMESPACE -l kubernetes.io/service-name=SERVICE -o yaml
steps.evidence: Compare Service selectors with Pod labels and endpoint readiness. Inspect readiness-probe failures before assuming a networking defect.
Correct selector mismatch or restore application readiness. Do not bypass readiness merely to make an endpoint appear.
Verify ready EndpointSlices and a successful request through the Service from an intended client.

references.title: Service has no ready backends — primary documentation

debugging.title: Service port mismatch
debugging.symptom: Pods are ready but connections through the Service fail.

steps.evidence: Compare port and targetPort with the actual container listener, including named-port resolution. Confirm endpoints before investigating policy.
Correct the Service mapping or application bind port and roll out the change in source.
Test the Service port and direct backend path from an authorized diagnostic client and confirm only intended exposure.

debugging.title: DNS blocked by egress policy
debugging.symptom: A workload loses name resolution after a restrictive policy rollout.

steps.evidence: Inspect policies selecting the Pod and the actual DNS path, including the cluster's DNS implementation. Confirm whether UDP/TCP DNS traffic is allowed as required.
Add narrowly scoped DNS egress compatible with the cluster design while retaining dependency restrictions.
Resolve required names from the workload and confirm unrelated outbound traffic remains blocked.

references.title: DNS blocked by egress policy — primary documentation

debugging.title: PVC remains Pending
debugging.symptom: A storage-backed workload cannot start because its claim is unbound.

steps.evidence: Inspect StorageClass, access mode, capacity, provisioner events and topology. WaitForFirstConsumer may intentionally defer binding until scheduling context exists.
Correct an invalid class/request or restore provisioner permissions/capacity. Do not create an arbitrary volume in the wrong zone.
Confirm binding, attachment, mount and an application-level read/write check on the intended durable storage.

debugging.title: HPA does not scale
debugging.symptom: An HPA stays at its current replica count during increased demand.

steps.evidence: Read conditions and metric status; check resource requests for utilization-based targets, bounds and stabilization. Verify the workload is horizontally scalable.
Restore missing metrics or requests, correct the target/bounds and address downstream limits. Raising max replicas alone may not help.
Apply representative load and verify replica changes, readiness and user latency while preserving dependency headroom.

references.title: HPA does not scale — primary documentation

debugging.title: Drain blocked by disruption budget
debugging.symptom: Node maintenance cannot evict a Pod.

steps.evidence: Compare budget selector, allowed disruptions, ready replicas and application quorum. An unavailable replica may leave no safe eviction capacity.
Restore readiness or add justified replicas before drain. Change the budget only when application availability semantics permit it.
Confirm a controlled eviction succeeds while required quorum and user service remain healthy.

references.title: Drain blocked by disruption budget — primary documentation

debugging.title: Rollout stalls on readiness
debugging.symptom: A Deployment creates new Pods but never becomes fully available.

steps.evidence: Inspect Deployment conditions, new ReplicaSet Pods and readiness logs. Check configuration, dependencies and surge capacity rather than increasing deadlines blindly.
Fix the failing revision or perform a compatible rollback. Correct probe design if it does not reflect actual readiness.
Verify rollout completion and representative user requests, including all replicas and any affected dependency paths.

references.title: Rollout stalls on readiness — primary documentation
